case_name: McGill University c. Students for Palestine's Honour and Resistance McGill
text:
McGill University c. Students
for Palestine's Honour and Resistance McGill

2024 QCCS 3857

SUPERIOR COURT

(Civil Division)

CANADA

PROVINCE OF QUEBEC

DISTRICT OF

montreal

No.:

500-17-131597-240

DATE:

October 21, 2024

_____________________________________________________________________

PRESIDING:
THE HONOURABLE GARY D.D. MORRISON, J.S.C.

_____________________________________________________________________

MCGILL UNIVERSITY

Plaintiff

v.

STUDENTS FOR PALESTINE’S
HONOUR AND RESISTANCE MCGILL

Defendant

_____________________________________________________________________

JUDGMENT

_____________________________________________________________________

No table of contents entries found.

INTRODUCTION

[
1
]

Plaintiff McGill University (“
McGill
”)
seeks again provisional injunctive relief against Defendant Students for
Palestine’s Honour and Resistance McGill (“
SPHR‑M
”)
[1]
.

[
2
]

An
ex parte
ten-day provisional
injunction was issued by judgment rendered on October 8, 2024 (the “
Judge
Barin Injunction
”), which was set to expire on Friday, October 18,
2024, the date of the hearing giving rise to the present judgement.

[
3
]

The Judge Barin Injunction was served on SPHR-M,
via Facebook, service by Instagram not being feasible
[2]
. All McGill staff and students
are purported to have been sent a description thereof and a link thereto by
means of an email
[3]
.
These issues of service are for information only and are not germaine to the
issue to be decided presently.

[
4
]

An
Amended Originating Application
, a
supplemental affidavit of Angela Campbell in support thereof, and an
Application
for a Special Mode of Service
, along with related affidavit and exhibits,
have all been more recently served to SPHR-M via Facebook and SPHR-M’s email
address
[4]
.

[
5
]

A Notice of Presentation

of an
Application
for a Safeguard Order to Renew the Order of Provisional Injunction
dated
October 11, 2024
[5]

was communicated to SPHR-M by Facebook on October 11, 2024, indicating a
presentation date of October 18, 2024
[6]
.

[
6
]

No one, whether individual or attorney, appeared
before the Court during the October 18
th
hearing purporting to
represent SPHR-M, as is confirmed in the Minutes of Hearing (“
procès-verbal”
).

[
7
]

However, counsel did attend at the hearing on
behalf of four entities
[7]

purporting to be “Intervening Parties”. However, they have filed no proceedings
for the purposes of what they describe as an aggressive intervention and,
accordingly, are not intervening parties within the meaning of the Quebec

Code of Civil Procedure
(“
C.C.P.
”).

[
8
]

Nonetheless, given the absence of Defendant
SPHR-M, the Court for purposes of public interest, did allow counsel to the four
entities that express a desire to intervene by way of aggressive intervention,
to make certain comments regarding the proposed injunction renewal, primarily
as regards its scope and the criteria of urgency.

(i)

The Judge Barin Injunction

[
9
]

Before proceeding further, it is useful to
understand the factual context that gave rise to the Judge Barin Injunction,
which he describes as follows
[8]
:

[7]

In its Originating Application, McGill
submits that since the attacks of Hamas on Israel on 7 October 2023, SPHR and
others have organized protests on the university’s campus to, among other
things, express their support for the Palestinian people. According to McGill,
while some of SPHR’s activities have been peaceful, a number have not, and they
have intimidated certain members of the university’s community.

[8]

The
protests have also, apparently, at times, interfered with the rights of McGill
students to learn and the employees to work in a peaceful, stable, and
harassment-free environment. For example, the university explains, in the past,
students, staff, and faculty were barred from entering classrooms and
buildings, and classes had to be cancelled or moved to online platforms for
safety reasons.

[9]

McGill
also submits that SPHR has organized a “Week of Rage” from 7 to 11 October
2024, to manifest its discontent with the way in which the university has
responded to its calls for divestment of investments and academic activities
tied to Israel. Based on SPHR’s past behaviour, in particular, the university
fears that the so called “Week of Rage” will seriously impede with the delivery
of courses and other activities that are essential to the academic program of
thousands of students and instructors on its campus.

[10]

This is why, McGill adds,
on 2 October 2024, it advised students, staff and faculty alike that between 5
and 7 October 2024, the university would temporarily put in place certain
security measures – including
restricting campus
access to current McGill students and employees and essential visitors, moving
all classes that do not need to be in person to online platforms, requiring
McGill-issued ID card access to enter buildings, and requiring all staff to
work from home, whenever possible
– so as to, among other reasons,
support their well-being, and seek to deter and prevent activities that violate
the law and its policies, such as those set out in McGill’s
Student
Code of Conduct
and the
Charter of Student Rights
that
apply only to students.

[
10
]

That “Week of Rage”, from October 7 to 11, 2024,
will be discussed later.

(ii)

The Nature of a Provisional Injunction

[
11
]

An injunction is an exceptional and
discretionary form of relief
[9]
.

[
12
]

Accordingly, the authority of the Court to issue
a provisional injunction in the case of urgency pursuant to Art. 509 and
following C.C.P., involves the exercise of a discretionary power.

[
13
]

That said, the injunction is to be viewed from
its prospective effect, meaning that it is not intended to punish for past
misconduct but rather to forbid a certain future conduct on pain of contempt of
court
[10]
.

[
14
]

The well-recognized criteria to be considered
are the applicant’s appearance of right, irreparable or serious harm, balance
of inconvenience and, given the provisional nature of the remedy, urgency that
the injunction be issued.

[
15
]

Given the urgent nature of a provisional injunction,
it can only be rendered for a period not exceeding 10 days, except if by
consent.

ANALYSIS
AND DISCUSSION

[
16
]

For the reasons that follow, the Court will not
issue the provisional injunction presently sought by McGill.

[
17
]

What the proposed injunction is meant to
prohibit is essentially the same conduct as in the Judge Barin Injunction,
being (without repeating verbatim):

-

blocking, obstructing or hindering, in whole or
in part, the entrances or exits to any buildings and streets directly connected
to entrances or exits of buildings on McGill University’s campus and any
buildings used for McGill’s operations;

-

protest activities within 5 metres of any
building on McGill’s campus, as well as any building used for McGill’s
operations, such protest activities including, amongst other things, setting up
tents or other structures, and making excessive noise;

-

intimidating, harassing and/or threatening any
student, employee, contractor or visitor of McGill while attempting to enter or
exit any of the buildings described above;

-

“disturbing the peace” or engaging in “public
disturbance” while inside or outside one of the above buildings, and, as well,
acting in a manner that “obstructs the delivery of courses or disturbs their
flow”.

[
18
]

The proposed injunction includes a mandatory
component requiring SPHR-M to publish the judgement granting the injunction on
its various social media pages.

[
19
]

As to “who” is being envisaged by the proposed
injunction, it is first and foremost the Defendant SPHR-M.

[
20
]

However, for each prohibitive order, after
identifying SPHR-M, McGill then adds “as well as any person having knowledge of
or having received service of the judgment”.

[
21
]

Although the broad scope as to who would fall
within the prohibitive orders, the Court understands that SPHR-M is not a
well-defined association but rather is an unincorporated and unregistered group
without juridical authority. It appears to describe itself as a “Student-run
organisation committed to the liberation of Palestine in its struggle against
Zionism and Imperialism”
[11]
,
as well as “a non-hierarchical club that champions the Palestinian liberation
struggle against setter-colonialism, apartheid and genocide, based on
principles of anti-colonial solidarity and social justice”
[12]
.

[
22
]

The Court further understands that SPHR-M is no
longer a club affiliated with the Students’ Society of McGill University, that
status having been revoked
[13]
.

[
23
]

Such groups can nevertheless be the subject of
an injunction
[14]
.
The Court need not, given its conclusion not to issue a provisional injunction,
address the practical issues of identifying who are members of such a group.

[
24
]

In the Court’s view, McGill satisfies, at this
provisional stage, the criteria required for the issuance of a provisional
injunction except for urgency.

[
25
]

The blockage and hinderance of entry to and exit
from building where courses are delivered or where McGill otherwise conducts
its operations, or where its visitors and contractors may attend as part of
courses or operations, especially in view of prior conduct over the course of
the fast few months
[15]

would, in the Court’s view at this stage, satisfy the appearance of right
criteria.

[
26
]

These comments would also apply to the criteria
of irreparable or serious harm, as such conduct and activities would seriously
interfere with McGill’s stated mission
[16]

and would also contravene its statement of principles regarding freedom of
peaceful assembly and the respectful expression of the diversity of opinions
[17]
.

[
27
]

For example, as described in a SPHR-M post
regarding events on October 7, 2024, it stated the following:

On October 7
th
,
thousands of students and community members rallied together and reclaimed our
campuses, smashing through McGill’s fences and flooding the lower field.
Despite the pre-announced shut down with private mercenaries and riot cops,
Montreal mobilized in its thousands to break through McGill’s fascist border
regime and demand divestment.

Protestors then targeted the
construction site of Zionist funded Sylvan Adam’s Sports Science Institute
(SASSI) which hopes to establish a permanent partnership with Tel-Aviv
University. The site was met with shattered glass and paint, affirming that
there will be no peace so long as McGill continues to partner with institutions
complicit in genocide.

On this monumental day, we loudly
affirm our commitment to the undying resistance of Palestine.

Until divestment and liberation,
the students of Montreal will never be silenced.

[
28
]

That text should be read in the context of the
video clips at Exhibits P‑25 and P‑31.

[
29
]

The prohibition as to intimidation, harassment
or threats directed at students, employees, contractors and visitors while
entering and exiting buildings on McGill’s campus or where it otherwise
conducts operations is also one to which McGill has an appearance of right, and
this for the same reasons.

[
30
]

As for the balance of inconvenience, there is no
absolute prohibition regarding protest activities other than within a stated
distance of 5 metres of buildings on McGill’s campus or otherwise were used for
its operations. That distance could be modified by the Court.

[
31
]

As well, that prohibition would also include
setting up tents and making excessive noise.

[
32
]

As a result, the injunction would not prohibit
peaceful protest activities, nor the respectful expression of different
opinions as opposed to intimidation, harassment or threats.

[
33
]

The balance of inconvenience accordingly favours
McGill.

[
34
]

That said, the Court would have modified various
conclusions so as to restrict certain overreach and uncertainties, however
given the Court’s intention to dismiss, that is not presently necessary.

[
35
]

This brings us back to the issue of urgency.

[
36
]

As mentioned when the Judge Barin Injunction was
issued on October 8, 2024, SPHR-M had announced a “Week of Rage” from October 7
to 11, 2024, and this corresponding to the one-year anniversary of the October
7
th
attack by Hamas on Southern Israel, which gave rise to the
government of Israel initiating its military response, which continues to this
day.

[
37
]

To be clear, the Court in issuing the Judge
Barin Injunction held as fact that SPHR‑M “glorified the attacks in a
social media post, describing the events as a ‘heroic attack’ and calling for
people to ‘celebrate the resistance’s success’”
[18]
.

[
38
]

This “Week of Rage” organized for October 7 to
11, 2024 followed months of activity by SPHR-M, as detailed in the Judge Barin
Injunction
[19]
.

[
39
]

In the days preceding October 7
th
,
McGill issued an email to students and staff announcing that it would put
certain security measures in place to deter and prevent unlawful activities, as
well as those that violate its policies
[20]
.

[
40
]

At the same time, McGill sought an
ex parte

provisional injunction, which was heard on October 7 and issued on October 8,
2024 for the maximum period of 10 days.

[
41
]

That was then. The Court must now assess the
situation as it currently exists.

[
42
]

To start with, there is an obvious and striking
difference with the situation as it presently exists in that the “Week of Rage”
has passed.

[
43
]

So, to what facts does McGill refer with a view
to justifying the criteria of urgency?

[
44
]

The Court takes into consideration the
Supplemental Affidavit dated October 15, 2024 of Angela Campbell, a full-time
professor in the Faculty of Law, member of that faculty since 2003, and Interim
Deputy Provost (Student Life and Learning) at McGill, particularly as regards
the facts subsequent to the issuance of the Judge Barin Injunction.

[
45
]

The Court understands that on October 9 and
October 12, 2024, SPHR-M published two posts on Instagram. The former
[21]
states that McGill’s Sylvain
Adams Sports Science Institute had met with shattered glass and paint,
affirming that “there will be no peace so long as McGill continues to partner
with institutions complicit in genocide”.

[
46
]

The second post is the video
[22]
that declares that they have
“resisted” two injunctions, that they cannot be repressed, that “THE STUDENT
INTIFADA CANNOT BE STOPPED” and that “we” must be “part of this revolution”,
all with various images, including vandalism committed to McGill’s buildings,
as attested to by Angela Campbell
[23]
.

[
47
]

Apart from these two posts describing events
immediately preceding the issuance of Judge Barin’s Injunction, the only other
factual event is described as follows
[24]
:

On or around the night of October
10
th
, 2024 and the early morning of October 11
th
, 2024,
the homes and/or the area around the homes of several senior McGill
administrators were targeted with graffiti, including the words “Fuck your
injunction.”

[
48
]

Notwithstanding such disturbing conduct, McGill
does not argue that either SPHR‑M or anyone else has contravened the
Judge Barin Injunction. Nor is McGill presently seeking an injunction in
relation to homes of its administrators.

[
49
]

The question, therefore, is whether the past
conduct of SPHR-M and its more recent declarations of an Intifada and a
revolution, with images from prior events, are sufficient to constitute
urgency. In the Court’s view, it is not.

[
50
]

If such circumstances alone did constitute
urgency, then such urgency could conceivably continue to exist
ad infinitum

without any additional acts by SPHR-M, and this simply by reason of past
conduct creating a fear or concern for some imminent yet uncertain future conduct.

[
51
]

But as stated above, injunctions are not
retrospective but prospective. They are not intended to punish for past
misconduct, as we are reminded by the Supreme Court of Canada in
Place des Arts
[25]
.

[
52
]

In addition, and as stated above, a provisional
injunction is for a maximum of 10 days, so the urgency must relate to that
short term period.

[
53
]

Moreover, from what the Court understands, at
this stage, the activities envisaged by the Judge Barin Injunction and mentioned
in of the current proposed injunction involve events for which advanced notice
was given by SPHR-M. No such advance notice is mentioned in the present
application by McGill.

[
54
]

The Court recognizes that certain SPHR-M posts
include references to the future by stating that the “Student Intifada” cannot
be stopped
[26]
,
that “[u]ntil divestment and liberation, the students of Montreal will never be
silenced”
[27]

and that “[w]e must not only stand firm against this genocide but actively
combat it”
[28]
.

[
55
]

However, unlike in some of the caselaw cited by
McGill, the Court cannot conclude, with the evidence currently in hand, that it
is probable that SPHR-M will, in the next ten (10) days, proceed to engage in
the very conduct that the proposed injunction intends to prohibit.

[
56
]

In the matter of
Zorchinsky
[29]
, Justice Urbas concluded that
“it is more than probable, if not highly probable” that such conduct would be
engaged in “next week”.

[
57
]

In
Federation CJA
[30]
, according to Justice Gaudet,
it involved events “
annoncées pour aujourd’hui ou les prochains jours
”.

[
58
]

In a subsequent decision in the same matter of
Federation
CJA
[31]
,
Justice Garin concluded that it involved “flash protests” organized
spontaneously or on very short notice, by which time it would be “too late” to
seek the Court’s protection. There is no evidence to that effect in the present
matter.

[
59
]

In
Université du Québec à Montréal (UQAM)
[32]
, Justice Gouin concludes that photos demonstrated that garbage
pails and other materials were still obstructing door windows and other windows
of the science building and its related complex, as well as passages and
cameras that were still obstructed
[33]
.

[
60
]

In the related matter of
Medvedovsky
[34]
, Justice Masse opined that
the required urgency was not established because the applicant did not
demonstrate the impossibility to access the location where the exams were to be
held, and further, that the fear of being blocked access was insufficient given
the facts.

[
61
]

Moreover, this is not the same situation as
where the Court is being asked to order the dismantling of an existing camp on
an owner’s grounds. In such cases, the camp actually exists and is, therefore,
not a simple theoretical possibility.

[
62
]

Finally, the Court also takes into account that
not all SPHR-M activities involve violence or intimidation.

[
63
]

Given the outcome, the Court considers the
Application
for a Special Mode of Service
to be moot and will not decide same.

FOR ALL
THESE REASONS, THE COURT:

[
64
]

DISMISSES
Plaintiff McGill’s application
to renew or issue a provisional injunction as detailed in its
Amended Originating
Application for the Issuance of Provisional, Interlocutory and Permanent Orders
of Injunction
, dated October 15, 2024;

[
65
]

THE WHOLE
, with
costs to follow suit.
